title: How Something Spreads
principle: The number of people each ill person passes it to is called R.

t: One person is ill. Whether that becomes an epidemic or nothing at all comes down to a single number.
The difference between one case and a national emergency is not luck. It is whether each infected person passes it to more than one other, and that ratio is a number you can estimate.
sub: More than one, and it grows. Less than one, and it dies out.
Everything else — masks, vaccines, closures — is an attempt to move that number below one.

question: Each ill person infects exactly one other. What happens?
If every case produces exactly one further case, what is the outcome?
options: It ticks along without growing or dying out
stages.outcome: It ticks along without growing or dying out
note: Commit. One is the knife edge, and everything about control is about which side of it you are on.

t: Watch one ill person turn into an outbreak, and watch it end.
One case in a thousand people. Watch it grow, peak and stop — and look at how many were never infected at all when it ended.
goal: It ran out of steam before it ran out of people.
It ended with hundreds never infected. An epidemic stops when it can no longer find people easily, not when it has run out of them.

t: Change how catchy it is and watch what that does to the shape.
Vary R₀ and observe both the peak and the final size. Note that the final size rises steeply between 1 and 3 and then saturates — almost everyone is infected either way above about 4.
goal: A bigger number makes it faster and bigger, but there is a limit to how much worse it can get.
R₀ controls both speed and final size, but the two saturate differently — above about R₀ = 4 nearly everyone is infected regardless, and the remaining effect is on how fast.

t: The number of people each ill person passes it to is called R.
R₀ is the average number of new cases produced by one case in a fully susceptible population. Above one it grows; below one it dies out.
R₀ = β/γ — transmission rate over recovery rate. It is not a property of the pathogen alone but of the pathogen in a particular population with particular behaviour.

That last point is routinely lost. R₀ depends on contact rates, so the same virus has different R₀ in a crowded city and a rural village, and quoted values are population-specific estimates rather than constants. Measles is usually given as 12–18 and even that is a range across settings.
sub: Below one and it dies out on its own. That is the whole aim.
Every control measure — vaccination, isolation, masks, closing schools — is an attempt to push R below one.
It falls on its own as people become immune, which is why epidemics end without anything being done.

The effective R falls as susceptibles are used up, so an unchecked epidemic ends by exhausting its own fuel. The overshoot is why: transmission continues past the threshold because there are still many infectious people, so the final size exceeds what the threshold alone would suggest.

q: Why does an epidemic stop before everyone has had it?
Why does an unchecked epidemic leave people uninfected?
Why does the epidemic end above rather than at the threshold?
options: Once enough people are immune, it cannot find new people fast enough
The germ gets weaker over time
why: As more people have had it, an ill person meets fewer people who can catch it. Once each one passes it to less than one other, it dies out — and there are still plenty of people who never got it.

Transmission requires susceptible contacts. Once the susceptible fraction falls below 1/R₀, each case produces fewer than one further case and the outbreak declines — with a substantial fraction never infected.

Because infectious people are still present when the threshold is crossed, so transmission continues while R is below one and declining. That overshoot means the final size exceeds the threshold, which is why an unchecked epidemic infects considerably more people than herd immunity strictly requires — and why reaching immunity by infection costs far more cases than reaching it by vaccination.

t: It is why closing schools or wearing masks works at all — each one takes a bit off that number.

No single measure has to stop transmission by itself. Each one removes some contacts, and they multiply: three measures each cutting transmission by a third take R from 3 to under 1 together. That is why control is usually a stack of partial measures rather than one decisive intervention, and why removing one can restore growth even though it never looked like it was doing much.
